newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Afghan woman weeps over future of daughters.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Afghan woman weeps over future of daughters.

text.p: Zaigull Hayan looked at her three daughters, their two female cousins and a woman friend from down the street and wept.

Many ordinary people are delighted that the purist Islamic Taleban movement has taken over Kabul and brought peace after years of war and terror. The ability to go out and be certain of coming home is a joy to many.
But Zaigull, 55, is not among them. She cannot go out.

"It's better to die than stay alive in the house. We are like birds in a cage," she said in her comfortable suburban home a week after the Taleban took the Afghan capital and told women to stay at home until a proper Moslem way was found for them to work and be educated.
"Everything I see around me makes me cry."
Zaigull never went to school but was determined her daughters would have the same opportunity in education as her son, now working in Germany.

She was well on the way to success. Nadia, 26, is a lawyer. Liva, 19, was studying language and literature at Kabul University and 13-year-old Wasima was doing well at school when the Taleban took Kabul and ousted a less purist government.

Cousin Shiwa, 21, was in the second year of her medical studies and wanted to be a doctor. Her sister, Sina, 23, was studying pharmacology and the friend from down the street, Soraya, 22, won a technical diploma and was working as a telephone engineer.
None of them expects to study or work again, even though the Taleban say they favour women's education and will find a way for that to continue and for women to work in complete separation from men.
Nadia said she did not believe them.
"They always say that, but they've been in control of places like Kandahar and Herat for a long time now and girls there don't go to school and women don't work," she said. "They're lying."

The Taleban have swept to power in about three-quarters of Afghanistan since their movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan. The southern city of Kandahar was their first base in Afghanistan and the supreme leader of the movement, Mullah Mohammed Omar, is still based there.
As in Kandahar and Herat, the first thing the Taleban did in Kabul was impose their vision of a pure Islamic life.
Television, music and drink were banned. Men were told they had six weeks to grow beards and must go to the mosque five times a day to pray.

Women were told to stay at home and that they could go out only if wearing the head-to-foot covering called a burqa, with a mesh over the eyes, and only if accompanied by a very close male relative like a father or a brother.

The Hayan women have no such close male relative living with them. They have not been outside the house since September 27, when the black-turbanned Taleban warriors swept into the city after a lightning attack. The previous government fled. Barely a shot was fired.
When Nadia went to school, a Soviet-backed communist government was in power. Educated women often wore modest dresses or jeans on the streets.
"We didn't like the communists because we are good Moslems, but at least women had the freedom to go to school and university and work," she said.
In 1992, the communist government collapsed and the mujahideen guerrillas, who had spent 13 years fighting it, took over.
"When the mujahideen came, girls and boys were separated on buses, at school and in offices and, of course, all females wore a headscarf. But we were still fairly free," Nadia said.
"Now the Taleban have come and I am shut up in the house. I don't know when I'll ever be able to go out again.

"We are kept like prisoners. If we did go out, they'll ask us why. We've heard that three women were beaten up by Taleban near here because they were out without a close male relative. We can't do anything but stay at home," Nadia said.

"The holy Koran says women can go out with their faces uncovered when there is trouble and they don't feel safe. That's how it is now, but the Taleban insist on full covering and a close male relative.

"I didn't get married because I wanted to complete my education and start my career first. Now I don't know whether I will ever be able to afford to get married. We're living on our savings and I don't know how long we can keep going like this."

The Hayan women rely on Zaigull's nephews to go to the bazaar to buy food. They spend all day in the house or the small, dusty garden in front of it behind the high wall of the compound typical of Afghan housing.

Western aid agencies estimate there are up to 45,000 widows who are the sole providers for their families in Kabul, a city partially destroyed in five years of fighting which cost many people almost all they had.
Wasima said her 12-year-old boy cousin's school re-opened on Saturday, but no teachers turned up. Most of them were women.

Wasima's school did not re-open. "I don't think it ever will. They don't want girls to go to school. I'm trying to study at home, but you can't do anywhere near as much in the house as you can at school."
Soraya, the medical student, said she had a hard time understanding why any government would not want women doctors.
"There just have to be women doctors and, if we can't go to university, how can there be women doctors to help all the women in this country who need a woman doctor," she said.
"But it's not just us. What about all the widows who have to work to look after their children? How are they going to manage now they aren't allowed to leave the house?"
